title: Load blood tubes into an analyser sample rack, each barcode facing its reader slot
instruction: Load the four blood tubes from the two bench racks into the analyser's sample rack, one tube per position. Stand each tube upright with its white barcode label facing out through its position's reader slot, in the rack wall nearest you, and let go of it. A label turned away from its slot cannot be read.
context: Laboratory instrument loading (Other: laboratory automation). Chemistry and haematology analysers in hospital and research laboratories take sample tubes in racks, loaded by hand tube by tube, and read each tube's barcode through a slot beside its rack position. Makers' instructions require the barcode to show through that slot (Beckman Coulter UniCel DxC job aid: "Ensure that bar code label is visible through the rack slot"; Abbott CELL-DYN 3200 manual: racks set so the reader reads the tube labels through the rack slots). A tube racked with its label turned away is a no-read, and its result waits for an operator. The hard part for a robot: positions are 28 mm apart, so a tube set down beside one already standing must be held with the fingers across the rack, and the grip taken at the pick must leave the label facing the slot after the wrist's quarter turn, turned the right way, without knocking the tubes already standing.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is the reference height. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint between them, z up from the table top; the arm bases are at y +30.5 cm and y -30.5 cm. (1) Analyser sample rack: dark grey rigid ABS plastic, held in place on the table (clamped in a real trial), which is its floor. Dimensions as modelled here (no maker's drawing used): one row of five square positions, each 24 x 24 mm inside, centred at x 30.0 cm and y +5.6, +2.8, 0, -2.8 and -5.6 cm (positions P1 to P5 from the robot's left), 28 mm apart, separated by 4 mm dividers inside 6 mm outer walls, all 40 mm tall; outside 36 mm front to back (x 28.2 to 31.8 cm) and 148 mm left to right. Five positions, as on the racks Roche cobas 6000 analysers take; sized for 16 mm tubes, which need no adapter (Beckman Coulter AU480/680 job aid: 13.6 to 16 mm). The wall nearest the arms (x 28.2 to 28.8 cm) has a reader slot in front of each position: 18 mm wide, centred on the position, open from 6 mm above the table to the top of the wall, so the lower part of a tube in that position shows through it from in front. Neighbouring tubes in the rack stand 12 mm apart. (2) Two bench tube racks of light grey rigid plastic, fixed to the table: each is 102 x 42 mm outside (x 17.9 to 28.1 cm) and 20 mm tall, with two square cells 30 x 30 mm inside, centred at x 20.0 and 26.0 cm, 6 mm outer walls and a solid 30 mm block between the cells; one rack is centred on y +20.0 cm (in front of the left arm), the other on y -20.0 cm. (3) Four blood collection tubes (10 mL K2EDTA type), loose, 20 g each (our estimate: tube and closure about 9 g plus a 10 mL fill), one standing upright in each bench rack cell: a 16 mm diameter clear plastic (PET) tube full of dark red liquid (blood; red-dyed water in a real trial), 82 mm tall, under a lavender closure 16.5 mm across and 18 mm tall (100 mm overall), with a white paper barcode label 10 mm wide on the side of the tube from 10 to 50 mm above its bottom (standing 1 mm proud of the tube in simulation, see fidelity). The labels face sideways at the start, a quarter turn away from the reader: the tube at x 20, y +20 cm faces its label to the robot's left (+y); the one at x 26, y +20 to the right (-y); x 20, y -20 to the right (-y); x 26, y -20 to the left (+y). Nothing else is on the table. Both arms start at the ready pose with the grippers open.
scoring: Scored on the state at the end of the trial. A tube is racked when it stands in one of the analyser rack's five positions: the centre of its bottom inside that position's 24 x 24 mm opening and within 5 mm of the table, its axis within 5 degrees of upright (standing on its own: a tube resting against a rack wall leans more than 8.6 degrees, the angle at which it tips), and no other tube's bottom in the same position (its centre inside that opening, within 5 mm of the table): with two tubes in one position, neither counts. A tube's label bearing is the direction the middle of its label faces (the label's outward normal), seen from above. A racked tube is readable when its label bearing is within 30 degrees of straight out through its position's reader slot, that is toward the arms (-x), and both vertical edges of its label's face lie inside that position's 18 mm slot (seen from in front, so no post hides any of the barcode), and it has been let go: neither gripper's finger zone (the space round the gripper's axis its pads can take at their present opening, from the pad tips 38 mm back) within 20 mm of it. Score 0.25 for each readable tube that is still (its bottom, its closure's top and its label's middle each moved 2 mm or less over the last 0.5 s). A racked tube whose label is turned away, sideways, toward the back wall or partly behind a slot post, earns nothing, as the analyser would skip it; so does a tube still held or touched by a gripper, a tube left in a bench rack, standing anywhere else on the table, lying down, upside down, leaning more than 5 degrees, above the rack's floor, dropped or off the table. Which tube goes in which position does not matter, and one position stays empty. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Success: all four tubes readable and still (score 1.0), held for 1 s. In a real trial each closure carries a black line across its top in line with the middle of its label (drawn when the label is put on), so a photo from above at the end shows which positions hold a tube, which way each label faces and that no finger is within 2 cm of a tube, and a photo from in front shows each barcode whole in its slot; a line near the limit is checked with a 60-degree sector template laid on the closure, pointed straight out through the slot, a lean with a protractor, a tube's bottom with a ruler.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, default friction. Each tube is one rigid body (tube, closure, label; no liquid). The label is a rigid 10 mm strip 1 mm proud so it shows from above (a real one is paper-thin and wraps further round; the strip stands for its barcode). Rack held in place, plain square positions, no spring clips (a tube can stand 4 mm off centre); the table is its floor; its dimensions are modelled, not from a drawing. No reader is simulated: readability is the label's bearing.
reset_notes: Stand each tube back upright in its bench rack cell with its label facing as in setup: x 20, y +20 cm to the robot's left (+y); x 26, y +20 cm to the right (-y); x 20, y -20 cm to the right; x 26, y -20 cm to the left. A pencil tick on each cell's side wall marks where its label (and its closure's top line) goes. Nothing is consumed (a real build uses sealed, water-filled tubes with printed labels over a drip tray, never real samples).
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (1,800 steps); demo: 1.0 (1,016 steps); one-arm left idle: 0.5; one-arm right idle: 0.5
